items.q: Why generate tool schemas from Pydantic models?
items.a: One source of truth: the same class **describes** the input to the model and **validates** it in your code, so they can't drift apart. Less hand-written JSON, fewer mistakes.
items.trap: Thinking the schema alone protects you. You still validate every input when it arrives (lesson 3).

items.q: The model returns two tool_use blocks. How do you respond?
items.a: Run both, then send **one** user message containing **two** `tool_result` blocks, each with its matching `tool_use_id`.
items.trap: Sending one message per result, or answering only the first call: the next request fails.

captions.text: One tool is easy to write by hand.
Six tools, each with a schema, a description, a permission and a timeout, is where
hand-written dictionaries start to break.
In this lesson, we'll organise many tools in one place, let Pydantic write the
schemas for us, and handle a model that asks for several tools at once.
You'll register tools with a decorator.
Generate strict JSON schemas from Pydantic classes.
Dispatch a tool call by its name.
And handle several tool calls in one turn.
First, what is a registry?
Think of a restaurant menu.
Every dish is listed once, with its name, description and price.
When an order comes in, the kitchen looks it up on the menu.
A tool registry is the menu for your agent.
Every tool is listed once, with its name, description, input form, permission, and
timeout.
When the model asks for a tool, your code looks it up there.
Why bother?
Because one list means one source of truth.
The definitions you send to the model, and the functions your code runs, can never
drift apart.
Here's how the project does it.
A Tool is a frozen dataclass that holds everything about one tool: its name,
description, the Pydantic class for its input, the function, its permission, its
timeout, and an optional confirmation text.
We'll use permission in lesson five.
The registry is just a dictionary, from the tool's name to its Tool object.
And tool is a decorator.
A decorator is a function that wraps another function.
This one doesn't change the function at all.
It just adds it to the registry, using the function's own name as the tool name.
Now one real tool.
First, the input as a Pydantic class.
A title between one and a hundred and twenty characters.
A due date, or None.
And a priority that must be low, normal, or high.
Then the decorator, with the description, the input class, and the permission:
write, because adding a task changes data.
And the function itself.
Notice that it receives an AddTask object, already checked, not a raw dictionary.
So inside the function, a dot due really is a date, and a dot priority really is one
of the three values.
Writing JSON schemas by hand is slow, and easy to get wrong.
So we let Pydantic write them.
Here's a note with a string title, a string text, a boolean pinned, and a colour
that must be yellow, blue, or green.
Schema for turns the class into a JSON schema.
Look at the right side: string, string, boolean, and an enum with the three colours.
Every field is required, and additional properties is false, which strict mode
needs.
How does it work inside?
Pydantic's schema contains a few keywords that strict tool schemas don't accept,
like maximum length.
So we remove them.
That's safe, because Pydantic still checks those limits when the input arrives.
This code walks through the schema and drops those keywords.
One detail: Pydantic adds a keyword called title, but our task also has a field
called title.
So property names are kept, always.
I actually got this wrong in my first version, and a test caught it: the title field
vanished.
Then, for every object, additional properties becomes false, and every field becomes
required.
Optional values, like the due date, are written as either a date or null.
And definitions builds the list for the API, from the registry.
Name, description, schema, and strict true, for every tool.
Here's the whole menu.
Six tools: add, list, complete and delete tasks, and add and search notes.
Each with its inputs, its permission, and its timeout.
One registry, so nothing can drift.
Next, parallel tool calls.
Imagine your table orders three dishes.
A good waiter takes all three orders in one trip, not one trip per dish.
A model can do the same.
When a request needs several independent things, one reply can contain several tool
use blocks.
Your code runs them all, and sends all the results back together.
The request asks for two tasks.
The reply contains two tool use blocks.
That's a parallel tool call.
We run each call in order, and each result keeps the ID of the call it answers:
offline zero one, and offline zero two.
And here's the rule developers often break: all the results go into one single user
message, not one message per result.
The next request sends three messages, and the last one holds both results.
Let's dry run the message list.
Message one, from the user: the request.
Message two, from the assistant: two tool use blocks, IDs zero one and zero two.
Message three, from the user: both tool results, zero one and zero two, together.
And the wrong way: two separate user messages, one per result.
Don't do that.
Keep the results together, in the same order as the calls.
Pause and work it out.
A request needs three tool calls.
The model asks for all three in its first reply, and then answers.
How many requests are sent?
And how many messages are in the list at the end?
Two requests.
And four messages: the user request, the assistant with three tool calls, the user
with three results, and the final answer.
Compare that with lesson three of Module 4, where one call per turn needed more
round trips.
Interview corner.
Why generate tool schemas from Pydantic models?
A good answer: one source of truth.
The same class describes the input to the model, and validates it in your code, so
the two can't drift apart.
And less hand-written JSON means fewer mistakes.
The trap: thinking the schema alone protects you.
You still validate every input when it arrives.
Follow-up: the model returns two tool use blocks.
How do you respond?
Run both, then send one user message, containing two tool results, each with its
matching ID.
The trap: one message per result, or answering only the first call.
The next request will fail.
Quick check.
A reply contains three tool use blocks.
What does the next user message contain?
Three tool result blocks, each with its matching ID, all in that one message.
Recap.
A registry lists every tool once, so there's one source of truth.
The tool decorator registers a function by its name.
Pydantic classes generate the strict schemas.
And for parallel calls, run them all, and return all the results in one message.
Next lesson: the model's input can still be wrong.
You'll validate every call, and turn mistakes into messages the model can fix.
